Content:
Remember that we equate [MATH: 0] to "False" and [MATH: 1] to "True." As well as conjunction, disjunction, negation, implication, and equivalence, there are a few more logical operations we should know:

Content:

| [MATH: x_1] | [MATH: x_2] | [MATH: x_1 \oplus x_2] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] |

The key difference between XOR and [MATH: x_1\lor x_2] is that XOR returns zero when [MATH: x_1 = x_2 = 1.] Hence, it is called the exclusive OR since it returns [MATH: 1] if [MATH: x_1] or [MATH: x_2] equal [MATH: 1,] but not both.
- The Peirce arrow (NOT OR or NOR) [MATH: x_1 \downarrow x_2] is true [MATH: (1)] if and only if both [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] are false [MATH: (0).] The corresponding Boolean function is the following:

| [MATH: x_1] | [MATH: x_2] | [MATH: x_1 \downarrow x_2] |
| [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |

| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 0] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] |

Note that the Peirce arrow is the negation of the Boolean OR operator:
[MATH: x_1 \downarrow x_2 = \lnot(x_1 \lor x_2)]

Content:
- The Sheffer stroke (NOT AND or NAND) [MATH: x_1 \mid x_2] is false [MATH: (0)] if and only if both [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] are true [MATH: (1).] The corresponding Boolean function is the following:

| [MATH: x_1] | [MATH: x_2] | [MATH: x_1 \mid x_2] |

| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: 1] |
| [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] |

The Sheffer stroke is the negation of the Boolean AND operator:
[MATH: x_1\mid x_2 = \lnot(x_1 \land x_2)]
